title: Restraint (360–365)
hook: restraint in eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, speech and mind is good

segments.voice: Yesterday, the best gift, and your line was the same: the best gift. Who did you share a teaching with? Day two hundred twenty-two, and chapter twenty-five, the mendicant.

Early morning in a town in Thailand, Laos or Sri Lanka. A line of monks in saffron robes walks slowly down the street, barefoot, eyes lowered, each holding a bowl. People wait on the curb with rice and fruit. The monks don't ask. They don't look around to see what's on offer. They stop, receive, and walk on in silence. It's one of the oldest daily scenes in the Buddhist world, and it's a picture of today's word, and of today's verses. Today: restraint.
screen: `A LINE OF SAFFRON ROBES.` → `BAREFOOT, EYES LOWERED, A BOWL.` → `THEY DON'T ASK.`

segments.voice: Today's word is bhikkhu, a Buddhist monk. A nun is a bhikkhuni. The word comes from bhikkha, alms, so a bhikkhu is literally one who lives on what is given. Max Müller used the Sanskrit form, bhikshu, and titled this chapter for him. The old commentaries add a second meaning, a play on sound: a bhikkhu is one who sees the danger in the round of rebirth. Chapter twenty-five describes the kind of person the word is meant to name, and it starts with the senses. Verse three hundred sixty, in Müller's English: "Restraint in the eye is good, good is restraint in the ear, in the nose restraint is good, good is restraint in the tongue." The next verse carries the list on: restraint in the body, in speech, in the mind, restraint in all things. The one restrained in all things, it says, is free of all pain. That's the monk on the alms round, eyes lowered, taking what comes. But restraint here isn't a cage. It's the frontier fort from last week, the guard at the gates. The verses go on to describe someone who controls hands and feet and speech, who is collected, content, and happy alone. Then a line about the mouth: the one who speaks wisely and calmly makes the teaching sweet. And a last piece of advice that fits anyone: don't look down on what you've received, and don't envy what others have received. A monk who envies others, the text says, doesn't find stillness. Monks and nuns keep this training full-time. Lay Buddhists keep a lighter version, especially on holy days, when many take extra precepts, like eating only before noon.
screen: `BHIKKHU — ONE WHO LIVES ON ALMS.` · `EYE, EAR, NOSE, TONGUE.` · `BODY, SPEECH, MIND.` · `DON'T ENVY WHAT OTHERS RECEIVE.` · then, large: `RESTRAINT IS GOOD.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let your eyes lower, the way the monks' do on the alms round. Don't close them yet. Just let your gaze rest on the floor in front of you, soft and still. Notice how the mind wants to look up, to see what's around. Let it want. Keep the gaze low. Then close your eyes, and notice the sounds coming in, without reaching out to name them. Receive what comes, like the bowl. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Bhikkhu. A Buddhist monk: one who lives on what is given, restrained in eye, ear, tongue, body, speech and mind.
Your line: restraint is good. Today, restrain one sense for an hour: no music, or no snacks, or eyes off the screens, and notice what the quiet gives back. Day two hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: In Theravada countries, monks walk an alms round each morning, receiving food in silence; lay Buddhists practice sense restraint more lightly, and on holy days many keep eight precepts, including eating only before noon.

match.prompt: match each piece of today's word and verses.
pairs: a monk, one who lives on alms

myth: bhikkhu comes from the word for alms
a bhikkhu is one who lives on what is given.
the verses stop at restraint of the eye and ear
they go on through nose, tongue, body, speech and mind: restraint in all things.
the chapter says envy of others' offerings is fine for monks

fork.setup: you're a monk on the morning alms round. a house ahead is clearly offering something delicious. what does the training say?
options: keep your eyes lowered and receive what comes.
fork.reveal: the verses praise restraint of the eye and the tongue, and warn against envying what others receive.

original.note: Pali bhikkhu (Sanskrit bhikṣu): a monk, one who lives on alms.

trapdoor: what you thought: a bhikkhu is a beggar.
what it means: a monk who lives on what is given, trained in restraint of every sense.
what a scholar hears: from bhikkha, alms; the commentaries add a sound-play, bhayam ikkhati, 'one who sees danger' in the round of rebirth.

sources.work: The Dhammapada (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 10)
